question: Why do you want to study Gender Studies?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific motivation grounded in real engagement with the field, not a vague statement about caring about equality.

bullets: Name a concrete moment, reading, or experience that pulled you toward the field
Show you understand it as an academic discipline with methods and debates, not just a cause
Connect the motivation to what you want to actually study or investigate
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I got interested after a school debate on the gender pay gap left me with more questions than the numbers could answer, so I started reading around it and realised the interesting part wasn't the statistic but how society built the conditions for it. That led me into bell hooks and then into the history of how 'women's work' got defined in the first place. I want to study Gender Studies because it lets me pull apart assumptions I used to think were just natural, using history, sociology, and law together rather than any one of them alone.

commonMistakes: Saying only 'I care about equality' with no academic substance
Treating the subject as activism rather than a discipline with methods
Giving an answer that could apply to any humanities subject
followUps: What's the difference between wanting to study this and wanting to campaign on it?

question: Why do you want to study Gender Studies here specifically, rather than at another university?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the specific course, its modules, faculty, or approach, not generic praise.

bullets: Reference a specific module, faculty member's work, or structural feature of the course
Explain why that feature matters to your particular interests
Show you compared it against alternatives and made a reasoned choice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Most programs I looked at treat Gender Studies as an add-on to sociology, but yours has a dedicated module on gender and law in the second year, which is exactly the intersection I want to focus on after a project I did on custody law. I also read some of Dr. Adeyemi's work on gender and migration policy, and the idea of being taught by someone actively researching that overlap is a big draw. I looked at two other courses that were more theory-only, and I chose this one because it keeps pushing you to apply the theory to real policy questions.

commonMistakes: Praise that could describe any university's program
Citing rankings or reputation with no specific detail
Not being able to name a single module or scholar
followUps: What would you want to contribute to seminar discussions here?

question: Was there a particular moment or experience that first drew you to thinking about gender?
lookingFor: A specific, honest personal account that shows reflective thinking rather than a rehearsed origin story.

bullets: Describe one concrete moment or experience, not a vague general awareness
Show what you actually did with that moment, such as reading or a project
Reflect on how your thinking has developed since then, not stayed static
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I noticed it clearly when my younger brother got told to 'toughen up' after crying at a film and I got told nothing at all for the same thing, and it struck me how differently we'd both been trained without anyone deciding to do it. That small moment sent me looking into how gender socialisation actually works, starting with a documentary and then some sociology texts our teacher recommended. What started as a personal observation turned into a genuine interest in how these patterns get reproduced across institutions like schools and workplaces.

commonMistakes: A generic answer with no specific memory attached
Stopping at the anecdote without showing what you did next
Overclaiming a dramatic personal story for effect
followUps: How has your view of that moment changed since then?

question: What's a book or piece of writing on gender that has influenced your thinking, and why?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine reading beyond the syllabus, with the ability to explain the argument and your own response to it.

bullets: Name a specific text and accurately summarise its central argument
Explain what you personally took from it or questioned about it
Show independent thought rather than just repeating the author's conclusions
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Audre Lorde's essays over the summer, particularly 'The Master's Tools Will Never Dismantle the Master's House,' and her argument that you can't fight oppression using the same frameworks that created it really stuck with me. It made me rethink an assumption I had, that reform within existing systems was always the safest route to change. I don't fully agree with every conclusion she draws, but the essay taught me to ask who a framework was originally built to serve before I use it.

commonMistakes: Naming a book without being able to describe its actual argument
Only summarising the text with no personal response
Picking a title to sound impressive rather than one you've genuinely read
followUps: What's a part of that argument you'd push back on?

question: How would you explain the difference between sex and gender to someone unfamiliar with the field?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate distinction between the two concepts, stated in plain language with an example.

bullets: Describe sex as generally referring to biological characteristics
Describe gender as the social and cultural roles, behaviours, and meanings attached to sex
Give a simple example that shows the distinction in practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sex usually refers to biological characteristics like chromosomes, hormones, and anatomy, while gender refers to the roles, behaviours, and expectations that a society attaches to those categories. So the colour associated with baby clothes isn't biological at all, it's a gendered meaning that a culture decided and that has actually changed over time and across countries. That's the basic distinction the field starts from, even though scholars debate how clean the line really is.

commonMistakes: Using the two terms interchangeably with no distinction
Giving a definition with no concrete example
Overcomplicating a basic explanation instead of being clear first
followUps: Where do you think that distinction gets complicated?

question: Can you explain what intersectionality means and why it matters in Gender Studies?
lookingFor: An accurate grasp of the concept, ideally with awareness of its origin, plus a concrete example of it in practice.

bullets: Explain that it looks at how overlapping identities like race, class, and gender combine to shape experience
Mention or gesture toward Kimberlé Crenshaw coining the term in legal scholarship
Give a concrete example showing why looking at gender alone can miss something important
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Intersectionality is the idea that categories like race, class, and gender don't act separately, they combine to shape a person's experience in ways you'd miss if you only looked at one at a time. Kimberlé Crenshaw introduced the term through a legal case where Black women weren't protected by discrimination law because the courts considered race and sex discrimination separately, and neither category alone fit their situation. It matters in the field because it stops us from treating 'women' as one uniform group, when a working-class woman of colour and a wealthy white woman can have very different relationships to the same policy.

commonMistakes: Defining it as simply 'multiple identities' with no explanation of the interaction
Not knowing where the term comes from at all
Giving no concrete example of it in action
followUps: Can you think of a policy that looks fair on gender alone but fails an intersectional test?

question: What do scholars in the field mean when they use the term 'patriarchy'?
lookingFor: An accurate, non-caricatured explanation of the term as a description of a social system, not a claim about individual men.

bullets: Describe it as a social system in which men hold disproportionate structural power and authority
Clarify it refers to structures and institutions, not every individual man
Offer an example of how it shows up institutionally, such as in inheritance law or leadership representation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Patriarchy refers to a social system in which men, particularly certain groups of men, hold disproportionate power in institutions like the family, government, and the economy, and where that power gets reinforced through norms and laws over time. It's a description of a structure, not an accusation against individual men, which is a distinction I think gets lost a lot in everyday conversation. A concrete example would be inheritance laws that historically passed property through the male line, which shaped who could accumulate wealth for generations regardless of any one person's intentions.

commonMistakes: Presenting it as an attack on individual men rather than a structural description
Giving a purely emotional definition with no institutional example
Confusing patriarchy with misogyny as if the terms mean the same thing
followUps: How do scholars argue patriarchy has changed over the last century?

question: Can you briefly outline what's meant by the different 'waves' of feminism?
lookingFor: A working knowledge of the wave framework and its rough historical focuses, plus awareness that the framework itself is debated.

bullets: Sketch the rough focus of first, second, and third (or fourth) wave feminism
Give at least one concrete historical example or figure
Show awareness that the wave metaphor is contested among scholars
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first wave, around the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, focused mainly on legal rights like suffrage and property ownership. The second wave, from the 1960s onward, broadened out to workplace equality, reproductive rights, and challenging domestic roles. Later waves brought in intersectionality and pushed back on the idea that earlier feminism had mostly centred white, middle-class women's experiences. I know the wave framework itself gets criticised for being too tidy and Western-centred, but it's still a useful starting map for the broad historical shifts.

commonMistakes: Listing the waves with no dates or examples attached
Treating the framework as an uncontested, settled fact
Confusing which issues belonged to which wave
followUps: What's a criticism of the wave framework itself?

question: Simone de Beauvoir wrote that 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' What do you think she meant by that?
lookingFor: An accurate reading of the claim as being about socialisation and construction of gender roles, with your own reflection on it.

bullets: Explain the claim as separating biological birth from the social process of becoming gendered
Note it's foundational to later social-constructionist thinking about gender
Add your own reflection or a limit you see in the argument
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read that as her saying womanhood isn't just a biological fact you're handed at birth, it's something built through upbringing, expectation, and constant social reinforcement, like how girls are taught to sit, speak, or want certain things. It's a founding idea behind later arguments that gender is constructed rather than fixed, which a lot of the field builds on. I find it a powerful claim, though I do wonder how it accounts for people who feel a strong, early sense of gender identity that doesn't seem to come purely from socialisation.

commonMistakes: Misreading the quote as denying biological sex exists at all
Reciting the quote with no actual interpretation offered
Giving no personal reflection or critique of the idea
followUps: How does this idea connect to later theorists like Judith Butler?

question: Judith Butler describes gender as 'performative.' What does that mean, and how is it different from saying gender is just a performance we choose?
lookingFor: Accurate grasp of a genuinely difficult theoretical concept, showing you understand it's not about conscious choice or acting.

bullets: Explain performativity as gender being produced through repeated acts, not expressed from an inner essence
Distinguish it from 'performance,' which implies a pre-existing self choosing to act
Give an example, such as repeated everyday gestures, that shows the constructed but not freely chosen nature of it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Butler's argument is that gender isn't an inner essence we then express outwardly, it's produced through the constant repetition of acts, gestures, and speech that we're trained into so thoroughly they feel natural. That's different from calling it a 'performance,' because performance implies a stable self behind the mask who is choosing to act a certain way, whereas performativity says there's no fixed self prior to those repeated acts at all. I think of it like the way we're praised as children for gender-typical behaviour so consistently that it stops feeling like behaviour and starts feeling like identity, even though nothing about it was ever freely chosen from a blank slate.

commonMistakes: Confusing performativity with 'gender is just an act people put on'
Treating it as meaning gender is a free, conscious daily choice
Reciting the term without any working explanation of the mechanism
followUps: What's a common misreading of Butler's argument that you'd want to correct?

question: Some people argue that gender differences are mostly biological, while the field often emphasises social construction. How would you approach that debate?
lookingFor: Balanced, informed reasoning that avoids dismissing either position outright and shows comfort with genuine academic disagreement.

bullets: Acknowledge that biology plays some role, without overstating or dismissing it
Explain why the field tends to emphasise how much social context shapes the meaning attached to any biological difference
Show you can hold the debate open rather than declaring one side simply wrong
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think it's productive to say biology plays no role at all, there's real research on hormones and development that shouldn't be waved away. But what the field pushes you to ask is how much of what we call 'natural' behaviour is actually shaped by what a culture rewards or punishes from birth, since the same biological starting point produces very different gender roles in different societies. I'd want to approach it by looking at specific evidence rather than picking a side on principle, because I think the honest answer is that biology and culture are tangled together in ways that are still being researched.

commonMistakes: Dismissing biological factors entirely as irrelevant
Treating social construction as an unquestionable fact rather than a scholarly framework
Refusing to engage with the tension at all
followUps: Can you think of cross-cultural evidence that complicates a purely biological explanation?

question: Is there a current gender-related issue in the news that you've been following closely? What's your take on it?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with contemporary debates, showing informed reasoning rather than reciting a slogan or headline.

bullets: Name a specific, real current issue rather than a vague generality
Show you understand more than one side or dimension of the debate
Offer your own reasoned view while acknowledging its complexity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been following the debate over paid parental leave policy in different countries, particularly how policies that offer leave only to mothers can end up reinforcing the assumption that caregiving is a woman's job by default. Countries that built in dedicated, non-transferable leave for fathers seem to have shifted that norm somewhat, though the data on how much actually changes at home is mixed. My own view is that policy design matters enormously here, a good intention like 'support parents' can still bake in old assumptions if you're not careful about the details.

commonMistakes: Naming an issue too vaguely to show real engagement
Only stating an opinion with no supporting reasoning
Ignoring any complexity or counterargument
followUps: What would you want to research further about that issue?

question: Why does Gender Studies also examine masculinity and men's experiences, not just women's?
lookingFor: Understanding that the field studies gender as a relational system affecting everyone, not solely women's issues.

bullets: Explain that gender is relational, so understanding masculinity is part of understanding the whole system
Give an example of how norms around masculinity also constrain men, such as around emotional expression or caregiving
Avoid framing the field as only about women
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Gender as a system doesn't only shape women, it shapes what's expected of men too, so you can't fully understand one half without the other. Research on masculinity looks at things like why men are underrepresented in caregiving professions or why boys are discouraged from expressing certain emotions, and those pressures have real costs, including on things like men's mental health outcomes. I think a common misconception is that the field is only 'about women,' when really it's about the whole relational system that produces both femininity and masculinity as categories.

commonMistakes: Treating the field as exclusively focused on women
Giving no concrete example of masculinity as a topic of study
Framing men's studies as somehow opposed to the rest of the field
followUps: Can you name a specific way traditional masculinity norms have been studied academically?

question: Gender Studies draws on many other disciplines. Which ones interest you most, and why?
lookingFor: Awareness that the field is interdisciplinary, with a genuine, specific interest in how particular disciplines contribute.

bullets: Name at least two disciplines the field draws from, such as sociology, history, law, or biology
Explain specifically what each contributes to studying gender
Show a personal preference or connection rather than listing them flatly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm most drawn to the overlap with history and law, because history shows you how gender norms have shifted and been contested over time, while law shows you how those norms get codified or challenged in concrete, enforceable ways. I also find the sociology side useful for understanding how norms get transmitted day to day through institutions like schools and families. What I like about the field is that no single discipline could really explain gender on its own, you need the historical, legal, and social angles together to get the full picture.

commonMistakes: Naming disciplines with no explanation of their specific contribution
Claiming interest in every discipline equally with no genuine preference
Describing the field as if it were purely one discipline in disguise
followUps: Which discipline do you feel least confident in, and how would you address that?

question: What do you hope to do after this degree, and how does studying Gender Studies prepare you for it?
lookingFor: A grounded, plausible direction connected honestly to the skills and knowledge the course actually builds.

bullets: Give a direction, not necessarily an exact job title
Connect it to specific skills the course develops, such as research, policy analysis, or critical writing
Show flexibility about how that direction might evolve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm drawn toward policy work, ideally around workplace equity or family policy, because that's where I think the analytical and research skills from this course would translate directly into real institutional change. The degree would give me practice reading data critically, understanding legal frameworks, and writing arguments that hold up under scrutiny, all of which policy work depends on. I know the exact role might look different once I'm further into the course and see what specialisations interest me most, but that's the general direction I'm aiming at.

commonMistakes: An overly vague answer with no connection to actual skills gained
An unrealistically specific plan with no room for growth
Suggesting the degree is only a stepping stone with no genuine interest in it
followUps: What specific skill from the course do you think matters most for that path?

question: Some people say Gender Studies isn't a 'real' academic subject. How would you respond to that?
lookingFor: A calm, evidence-based response that addresses the criticism directly rather than getting defensive or dismissive.

bullets: Address the criticism directly rather than avoiding or getting defensive about it
Point to the field's actual methods, evidence base, and rigor
Acknowledge honestly where the field does get things wrong or overreach, without conceding the whole premise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd say that criticism usually comes from picturing the field as pure opinion, when in practice it involves the same historical archives, legal analysis, and empirical sociology used across the humanities and social sciences, just applied to a specific set of questions. Like any field it has internal debates and sometimes gets things wrong or overreaches, and I think being honest about that actually strengthens the case rather than weakening it. I'd rather engage with the specific critique someone has than dismiss it, because usually there's a real question underneath about rigor that's worth taking seriously.

commonMistakes: Getting defensive or dismissing the critic instead of engaging with the point
Refusing to admit the field has any genuine internal debates or flaws
Giving a purely emotional response with no reference to methods or evidence
followUps: What's a genuine internal debate within the field you find compelling?

question: Has a film, documentary, or podcast about gender changed the way you think about anything?
lookingFor: A specific example with a clear, honest account of what changed in your thinking, not just a title dropped for effect.

bullets: Name a specific piece of media accurately
Describe the actual idea or scene that affected you
Explain concretely how your thinking shifted afterward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I watched a documentary on the history of the marriage bar, where women in some countries were legally required to leave certain jobs once they married, and I hadn't realised how recent and widespread that practice was. It changed how I think about workplace gender gaps today, because I used to assume they were mostly about individual choices, and it made me look harder for the institutional history behind patterns that get described as 'just how things are.' Since then I try to ask what legal or institutional history sits behind a gender pattern before assuming it's natural.

commonMistakes: Naming a title with no real detail about its content
Claiming a change in thinking with no explanation of what actually shifted
Choosing something clearly unwatched, just to sound well-read
followUps: What questions did it leave you with?

question: The field has been criticised for historically centring Western, white, middle-class experiences of gender. How would you make sure your own thinking accounts for that?
lookingFor: Awareness of a genuine and important internal critique of the field, with a thoughtful sense of how to guard against it in your own work.

bullets: Show awareness that early Western feminist scholarship often generalised from a narrow experience
Reference or gesture toward critiques from postcolonial or Global South scholars
Describe a concrete practice, such as seeking out non-Western sources, to counter the bias in your own thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of early Western feminist writing assumed its own conditions, like the specific pressures of white, middle-class domestic life, were universal, and scholars like Chandra Talpade Mohanty have written powerfully about how that flattened the experiences of women in the Global South into one passive category. For my own thinking, I try to actively look for scholarship written from within the context being discussed rather than relying on outside interpretations of it, and to ask whether a framework I'm applying was actually built with that context in mind. It's something I know I'll get wrong sometimes, but I'd rather stay alert to the risk than assume my starting assumptions are neutral.

commonMistakes: Denying the field has ever had this problem
Naming the critique with no idea how to actually address it in practice
Overcorrecting into assuming Western frameworks are never useful at all
followUps: Can you name a non-Western scholar or text whose work addresses this critique?

question: How would you explain the causes behind the gender pay gap to someone who thinks it's simply due to personal career choices?
lookingFor: An answer that engages seriously with the 'choice' argument while showing the structural factors that shape those choices.

bullets: Acknowledge that individual choices do play some role, rather than dismissing the point outright
Explain how structural factors, like occupational segregation or unpaid caregiving expectations, shape those choices
Give a concrete example or statistic-style point that illustrates the structural angle
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's true that choices about career path and hours worked do factor into the raw pay gap, so I wouldn't dismiss that entirely. But the more interesting question is why those choices split so consistently along gender lines, and a lot of research points to structural pressures, like women disproportionately taking on unpaid caregiving work, or certain fields becoming lower-paid specifically as they become feminised over time, which has happened historically in fields like teaching. So I'd say it's less that 'choice' is a myth and more that the choices themselves are shaped by conditions that aren't equally distributed to begin with.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the 'personal choice' framing outright with no engagement
Treating the pay gap as having one single, simple cause
Giving no concrete example of a structural factor
followUps: What's an example of a field becoming lower paid as it became feminised?

question: How do Gender Studies and Queer Studies relate to each other, in your understanding?
lookingFor: A working understanding that the two fields overlap substantially but aren't identical, with some sense of their distinct focuses.

bullets: Explain that Gender Studies examines gender broadly while Queer Studies focuses more specifically on sexuality and non-normative identities
Note the substantial overlap and shared theoretical roots between the two
Avoid collapsing them into being exactly the same field
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: They overlap a great deal and share a lot of theoretical ground, since thinkers like Judith Butler are central to both, but I understand Gender Studies as the broader field looking at gender as a category generally, including things like masculinity, motherhood, or gendered labour, while Queer Studies focuses more specifically on sexuality and identities that sit outside heterosexual and cisgender norms. They're not separate in practice, most programs blend them, but I don't think they're exactly the same thing either. I'm interested in both, though I'm probably more drawn to the broader gender and institutions side of it.

commonMistakes: Treating the two fields as completely identical with no distinction
Treating them as entirely unrelated to each other
Showing no awareness of shared theoretical figures like Butler
followUps: Which side are you more personally drawn to, and why?

question: Why do scholars in this field often argue that gender-based violence needs to be understood as a structural issue rather than a series of isolated incidents?
lookingFor: Understanding of the structural framing of gender-based violence, with sensitivity and a grasp of the policy implications.

bullets: Explain the argument that patterns of violence reflect broader norms about power and gender, not just individual bad actors
Note how this framing shapes different policy responses, such as prevention and education, not only punishment
Handle the topic with appropriate seriousness and care
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If you treat every incident as an isolated, individual failure, the response tends to focus only on punishing that one person after the fact. But scholars point out that the sheer consistency of who experiences this violence and who perpetrates it, and the way certain norms around control or entitlement get culturally reinforced, suggests something more structural is going on. That framing matters because it changes the policy response, it pushes toward prevention, education, and challenging the norms themselves, rather than treating it purely as a matter of individual criminal justice after the harm has already happened.

commonMistakes: Treating the topic too casually or without appropriate seriousness
Reducing the structural argument to blaming all individuals of one group
Giving no sense of what different policy responses follow from this framing
followUps: What's an example of a prevention-focused policy approach you're aware of?

question: Gender Studies uses both quantitative and qualitative research methods. Can you give an example of each, and why you'd choose one over the other?
lookingFor: Basic methodological literacy, showing you understand the field involves rigorous evidence gathering, not just argument.

bullets: Give a concrete example of quantitative research, such as survey data or wage statistics
Give a concrete example of qualitative research, such as interviews or ethnography
Explain a reason you might choose one approach over the other for a given question
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A quantitative approach might be analysing large-scale survey data to measure how attitudes toward parental leave have shifted over a decade across different countries, which is useful for spotting broad patterns and trends. A qualitative approach might be conducting in-depth interviews with new fathers about their actual experience taking leave, which captures nuance and lived experience that a survey question can't fully reach. I'd lean toward quantitative methods if I wanted to establish that a pattern exists broadly, and qualitative methods if I wanted to understand why it happens or how it actually feels to live through it.

commonMistakes: Only naming one method type and ignoring the other
Giving vague examples with no actual research design in mind
Suggesting one method is simply superior to the other in all cases
followUps: What are the limits of relying only on survey data for this kind of question?

question: This field includes genuinely contested debates, such as around trans inclusion and the definition of sex and gender. How would you approach discussing a topic like that in an academic seminar?
lookingFor: Maturity and intellectual rigor in how you'd approach a genuinely contested topic, not a personal political statement.

bullets: Emphasise engaging with the strongest form of different scholarly positions, not caricatures of them
Show respect for the seriousness and real stakes of the debate for the people it affects
Focus on the academic skill of evidence-based argument rather than declaring a settled personal verdict
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to go in prepared to actually read the different positions people hold in their strongest form, rather than the version of them that's easiest to dismiss, because I think a lot of public debate on this topic collapses into caricature on all sides. I'd also want to stay aware that this isn't a purely abstract academic exercise for a lot of people, it touches real lives, so I'd try to hold rigor and care together rather than treating it as a debate-club exercise. My aim in a seminar would be to understand the evidence and reasoning behind different scholarly positions clearly enough to explain them fairly, even the ones I don't personally land on.

commonMistakes: Dodging the question entirely with no substantive answer
Treating it purely as an abstract debate with no acknowledgment of real stakes
Presenting only one side as if it were the only legitimate scholarly position
followUps: How would you handle a seminar where classmates strongly disagreed with each other on this?

question: What do you think is the role of men in engaging with Gender Studies and gender equity issues?
lookingFor: A thoughtful answer that avoids both dismissing men's role and centring it inappropriately, showing balanced understanding.

bullets: Recognise that men have a genuine stake in gender norms and their effects, not just an outside obligation to help
Avoid framing it as men needing to 'save' or speak over the field
Suggest a concrete, appropriate mode of engagement, such as listening, supporting, and examining their own position
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think men have a real stake in this, not just as allies from the outside, since gender norms shape men's lives too, around things like emotional expression or caregiving expectations, so it's not purely an act of charity to engage with the field. At the same time, I think the most useful role is usually listening and supporting rather than trying to lead or dominate conversations that have historically excluded other voices. For me personally, being interested in this field means being willing to examine my own assumptions honestly, not positioning myself as the field's spokesperson.

commonMistakes: Framing men's involvement purely as heroic rescue of others
Suggesting men have no legitimate stake in the topic at all
Giving an abstract answer with no concrete sense of appropriate engagement
followUps: Can you think of a time you had to check your own assumptions on this topic?

question: Have you had any experience, through volunteering, a project, or a club, that's relevant to Gender Studies?
lookingFor: A specific, honest account of relevant experience with reflection on what you learned from it, not just a resume line.

bullets: Describe a specific, real activity rather than a vague general claim
Explain your actual role and what you did
Reflect on a specific insight or skill it gave you relevant to the field
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I volunteered for a year with a local organisation that supports women re-entering the workforce after long career breaks, mostly helping with interview prep and CV workshops. Sitting in on those sessions, I noticed how often the gap in someone's resume was actually caregiving work that had no formal recognition at all, which connected directly to things I'd been reading about how unpaid labour gets treated as invisible. It gave me a much more grounded sense of how abstract ideas about gendered labour actually play out in someone's real, practical life.

commonMistakes: Naming an activity with no specifics about your actual role
Choosing an experience with no genuine connection to the field
Listing the activity with no reflection on what it taught you
followUps: What would you do differently if you ran that project yourself?
